newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament to vote on taxes in two weeks.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament to vote on taxes in two weeks.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament will vote in two weeks on a package of bills that maintain this year's income tax levels in 1997, scrap an import tax and keep capital gains tax-free until the year 2000.

The house's press office said on Friday legislators had proposed so many amendments to the tax bills during their second reading on Wednesday that the budgetary committee decided it needed time to scrutinise them.
"Voting will take place at parliament's next sesssion in two weeks," a press officer said.

The government's bills orginally provided for lowering personal income tax levels to 20, 32 and 43 percent, depending on income, from the current 21, 33 and 45 percent already next year but committees recomended postponing the cut until 1998.
The committees argued Poland could not afford tax cuts next year because it faced increased spending for pension rises, education and health care systems.

The cabinet endorsed this view despite objections from Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko, whose tax cuts proposal was part of a mid-term plan aimed at maintainig economic growth at at least five percent annualy and radically slashing inflation.
The committees and the government agreed that personal income tax levels would be lowered to 21, 32 and 44 percent in 1998 and to 20, 30 and 40 percent in 1999.

They also delayed cuts in corporate tax planned by Kolodko. They proposed that the tax would be cut to 38 percent from the current 40 percent in 1998 and not next year as assumed by Kolodko's plan. It will later be reduced by two points annualy to reach 32 percent in 2001.
The cuts will be accompanied by the liquidation of some tax reliefs already in 1997.
The bills also provide for abandoning the current flat three-percent tax on all imported goods and maintaining tax-exemption for capital gains until the year 2000.

The first measure was enforced by Poland's entry the Organisation for the European Cooperation and Development (OECD) earlier this year while the second is meant to stimulate the country' fledging stock market.

The package, which still needs to clear both the lower house and the Senate and be signed by President Aleksander Kwasniewski, has been criticised by the opposition to the ruling leftist coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party.
The centrist Union for Freedom party charged that the parties had refused to lower taxes to boost spending on social programmes next year to win votes in the general elections due late in 1997.
